quote: The new flour is almost certainly not killing your starter.
Bran particles cut through the gluten strands and bring extra enzymes and minerals, which speeds fermentation up.
Weeks without feeding, which makes a starter acidic and slow rather than dead.
Fermentation is very temperature sensitive: dough that peaks in five hours at 24 C (75 F) can need eight or more at 20 C (68 F).
A different brand of wheat flour does not kill a starter.
Whole-grain or higher-extraction flour (more bran and germ left in) ferments faster, because it carries more nutrients and enzymes.
Sustained heat above roughly 50 C (120 F), weeks with no feeding, or visible fuzzy mold. A flour brand is not on that list.
note: lists prolonged non-feeding itself, unqualified, as something that kills the starter, with no hungry-not-dead qualifier anywhere in the reply

quote: Fermentation speed roughly halves for every 10 C (18 F) the dough cools, within normal kitchen range.
A new flour brand almost certainly did not kill your starter.
If the old bag was whole wheat or rye and the new one is white, you removed most of the minerals, enzymes, and bran-borne microbes.
note: framed as removal-slows-it, the converse of whole-grain-speeds-it, not a contradiction

quote: Bleached flour ferments somewhat slower than unbleached.
Gray liquid on top and a nail-polish or acetone smell mean hungry, not dead.
note: kill list also names 'weeks of neglect at room temperature' unqualified, in tension with this sentence; the explicit hungry-not-dead statement is the dominant, final word

quote: a kitchen that slid from 78F to 68F can easily double your timings with no flour involved at all
Flour brands do not kill sourdough starters.
Add 20 to 25 percent whole wheat or rye to every feeding, which supplies minerals and enzymes that white flour is stripped of.
Bleached all-purpose still works, just less vigorously.
Fuzzy growth in pink, orange, or black is mold, and that is the only case that calls for discarding and starting over.
Kitchen temperature dominates everything else; fermentation roughly halves in speed for every 15F drop.
